President Donald Trump’s vow to hand out $5,000 checks if Republicans hold on to control of both chambers of Congress in the midterm elections raises an immediate question: Can he really do that?
Trump announced his idea to send payments to “every adult” in a speech Wednesday at the Republican National Committee’s midterm convention in Dallas.
“Here is my promise,” he said. “If the Republicans win the House of Representatives and the United States Senate, both of them … because of our tremendous strength and success economically, I will issue a dividend to every adult citizen in the United States of America for $5,000, very much like a successful company will do a cash distribution to its shareholders.”
The proposal would only have one other “caveat,” Trump said, which is that the money must be spent in the U.S.
As of Thursday afternoon, the administration hadn’t shared details about how the funds would be distributed with this restriction. But there are several reasons to be skeptical that any money is coming your way.
Since the three rounds of pandemic-era stimulus checks, promises from politicians — namely Trump — to send direct payments to Americans have mostly gone unfulfilled. About 1.5 million members of the military received $1,776 “Warrior Dividends” last year, but remember those $5,000 DOGE checks floated in February 2025? They never materialized.
This time around may not be any different.
First, in order for the president to pursue these proposed payouts (per his terms), Republicans would have to dominate the midterms. The odds of a Republican House and a Republican Senate emerging from November’s elections are only 14% on Polymarket and 16% on Kalshi, the two leading prediction markets.
Trump acknowledged that his party has its work cut out for it as he announced the plan for “Trump dividends.”
“We might not win,” he said. “You win with us, and you get $5,000.” Later in the speech, he sounded more optimistic, saying, “We’re going to give you that Trump dividend of $5,000 if we win — and we’re going to win.”
However, even assuming the GOP retains majorities in both chambers, it’s still unlikely you’ll receive a $5,000 payout.
The main issue is a lack of enthusiasm among Republicans in Congress for more stimulus checks. Broadly speaking, fiscal conservatives do not want to add to the $40 trillion national debt with direct payments, and the price tag for these checks would be about $1 trillion. A precise cost cannot be estimated as the administration hasn’t shared information about a potential exclusion for the wealthy, as mentioned by Vice President JD Vance.
Will Congress approve $5,000 ‘Trump dividends’?
The Constitution gives Congress the power of the purse, which means sending $5,000 checks would require House and Senate approval.
DOGE checks and previously proposed tariff checks never advanced in large part because GOP congressional leaders like Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., opposed them, as did some rank-and-file Republicans and essentially all Democrats. Hoping for a different outcome this time, Sen. Bernie Moreno, R-Ohio, said that he will introduce a bill to try to deliver Trump’s $5,000 checks.
Democrats blasted the plan as unlawful and financially reckless.
“Actually, only Congress can make that promise since it must appropriate those funds. And Congress would never do it because it is corrupt and blatantly illegal,” Rep. Daniel Goldman, D-N.Y., wrote in a response on X.
California Gov. Gavin Newsom accused Trump of trying to “buy your vote,” while economist Peter Schiff called the move a “bribe.”
Fox News’ Bret Baier asked Vance in an interview after Trump’s speech how he responds to criticism from opponents that the president is “bribing voters to vote for Republicans” and risking more inflation. In response, Vance suggested the checks could be paid for with revenue from the Trump administration’s tariffs.
“If you keep us in power,” he said, “then you’re going to share in some of the benefit of this incredible wealth that we’re creating.”
Still, U.S. code states that it’s against the law “to make an expenditure to any person, either to vote or withhold his vote, or to vote for or against any candidate.” It’s unclear how courts might view the unprecedented $5,000 dividend proposal that Trump has announced if legal challenges arise.

Trump pledges $5,000 payment to every American adult if Republicans hold Congress in 2026
President Trump promised a $5,000 cash payment to every adult citizen in the country, but only if voters keep Republicans in control of both the House and Senate this November, a proposal critics say would pile more than a trillion dollars onto the national debt.
Trump unveiled the pledge during a 107-minute keynote address at the Republican National Committee's first-ever midterm convention, held at the American Airlines Center in Dallas on September 9. He called it the "Trump Dividend" and framed it the way a corporation frames a cash distribution to shareholders, in this case, with the American public cast as the shareholders of a country he says is finally turning a profit.
The New York Post reported that the dividend announcement served as the centerpiece of a sweeping speech in which Trump laid out a legislative agenda for his final two years in office, telling the crowd he needs a Republican Congress to "finish the job."
Trump ties the payout directly to a GOP midterm victory
The president left no ambiguity about the condition. The Washington Examiner reported that Trump made the promise contingent on Republicans winning both chambers of Congress in the November 3 election, not one chamber, both.
Trump put it plainly from the stage:
"If the Republicans win the House of Representatives and the United States Senate, both of them... I will issue a dividend to every adult citizen in the United States of America for $5,000."
He followed that with a line aimed squarely at turnout: "We're going to give you that Trump dividend to $5,000 if we win, and we're going to win."
There was one stipulation beyond the election result. Trump said the money must be spent inside the United States, not in foreign countries. As Breitbart reported, the president framed that requirement as a way to ensure the cash cycles back through the American economy rather than flowing overseas.
"The only caveat I have is that the dividend that we're making must be spent in the United States of America," Trump said.
A $1.2 trillion price tag lands on a $40 trillion debt
The math is straightforward and large. Roughly 240 million adults hold U.S. citizenship. At $5,000 each, the total cost would exceed $1.2 trillion, a figure that would land on top of a national debt already at $40 trillion and an annual federal deficit running near $2 trillion.
The proposal would also require an act of Congress. No president can unilaterally authorize payments of that scale. That means even with a Republican majority, the dividend would need to clear committees, survive floor votes, and navigate the Senate's procedural hurdles before a single check could go out. Trump's administration has shown a willingness to push ambitious policy through Congress, from executive moves reshaping the meat industry to major trade deals, but a $1.2 trillion spending bill is a different order of magnitude.
Vice President JD Vance offered a partial answer on the funding question. Fox News reported that Vance suggested wealthy Americans could be excluded from the payments, which would reduce the overall cost. He also pointed to tariff revenue as a potential funding source, calling the proposal "fundamentally a dividend for American workers."
"What the president is talking about is fundamentally a dividend for American workers."
Trump himself echoed the tariff argument, framing the dividend as something Democrats could never deliver because they oppose the trade policies generating the revenue. It is a political argument as much as a fiscal one, positioning the payout as a reward for voters who back the party that imposed tariffs, not the party that fought them.
Fiscal hawks raise alarms over the deficit math
Not everyone on the right was cheering. Marc Goldwein of the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget, a nonpartisan fiscal watchdog, pushed back hard on the premise that the government has money to distribute.
AP News quoted Goldwein directly:
"The idea that we've had fiscal success is backwards and bordering on laughable. We don't have surpluses to give away."
That criticism cuts at the core tension in the proposal. Trump is framing the dividend as a return on good governance, the country is doing well, so citizens deserve a share. Goldwein and others argue the books do not support that framing. A $2 trillion annual deficit means the government is borrowing to cover its existing obligations, let alone a new $1.2 trillion outlay. Any dividend paid under those conditions would be funded by debt, not by surplus.
The question of whether tariff revenue can cover the gap remains unanswered. Tariffs have created significant new revenue under the Trump administration, but the total collected falls well short of $1.2 trillion. Vance's suggestion that excluding wealthy recipients would lower the cost is plausible on paper, but no income threshold or eligibility framework has been announced. The details, who qualifies, how the money moves, and what legislation would authorize it, remain open.
Trump has not been shy about making bold economic promises during his time in office. His administration has pursued major international energy deals and pushed policy changes that previous administrations avoided. Whether this pledge follows the same pattern, an ambitious opening bid that gets refined through the legislative process, or stands as a campaign-trail commitment that fades after Election Day will depend on what happens in November and what happens in January.
Midterm strategy built on a direct offer to voters
Strip away the fiscal debate and the political logic is clear. Midterm elections historically punish the president's party. Turnout drops. The opposition is energized. The governing party loses seats. Trump is trying to reverse that gravity by giving voters a concrete, personal reason to show up, not an abstract policy argument, but a dollar figure with their name on it.
The structure of the promise reinforces the point. It is not a tax cut that shows up gradually in paychecks. It is not a regulatory change that benefits businesses and eventually trickles down. It is a check. Five thousand dollars. Singling out adult citizens, not corporations, not institutions, not foreign governments, sends a message that the administration sees ordinary Americans as the primary beneficiaries of its economic policies.
Democrats face an awkward counter-messaging problem. Opposing a $5,000 payment to every American adult is a difficult position to hold in public, especially when House Democrats have struggled to define what they stand for heading into the midterms. Attacking the proposal on fiscal grounds risks sounding like the party cares more about spreadsheets than kitchen tables. Ignoring it risks letting Trump own the economic narrative for the final stretch of the campaign.
The president's willingness to make this kind of direct, transactional appeal also reflects confidence, or at least projected confidence, in the Republican position heading into November. Historically, a president who believes his party is about to lose seats does not make promises that require holding both chambers. Trump is betting publicly that the GOP can defy midterm gravity, and he is putting a price tag on what voters get if he is right.
That bet carries risk. If Republicans lose even one chamber, the promise evaporates, and Trump owns a broken commitment heading into the final stretch of his presidency. The administration has faced legal and political resistance on other fronts, federal judges have blocked executive actions and policy reversals have drawn opposition, but a failed dividend promise would be uniquely personal. Every voter who expected $5,000 and did not get it would remember why.
Open questions the White House has not answered
Several critical details remain unresolved. No legislation has been introduced. No executive order has been drafted. No income threshold for eligibility has been set, despite Vance's suggestion that wealthy Americans might be excluded. The mechanism for distributing payments, whether through the IRS, Treasury, or some new system, has not been described. And the timeline for when Americans would actually receive the money, assuming all conditions are met, is unknown.
Those gaps matter. A promise without a policy framework is a campaign pledge, not a governing plan. Congress would need to pen, debate, and pass authorizing legislation. The Congressional Budget Office would score the cost. Senate rules could require 60 votes or allow passage through reconciliation with a simple majority. None of those procedural realities have been addressed publicly.
The promise is bold, specific, and easy to understand, which is exactly what makes it effective as a political tool and exactly what makes the unanswered questions so important. Five thousand dollars is real money to most American families. If the proposal is serious, voters deserve to know how it works. If it is a negotiating position, an opening bid designed to be refined, the administration should say so.
Washington has no shortage of politicians who promise checks and deliver excuses. If Trump means this one, the details need to follow the headline, before November, not after.

"If the Republicans win, you win with us and you get $5,000" - that's what President Donald Trump is promising US voters ahead of the November midterm elections.
The "Trump dividend" - as it's called - would give every American adult the payout - IF the Republicans retain control of the U.S. House and Senate.
President Trump says it's "really good" - and would be a "great infusion".
But it's receiving pushback from others in the U.S. - Marc Goldwein, from the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget, says this would cost one-point-two trillion USD in just one year.
And some have raised concerns the payment could break election law.
So, can Trump really pay every American this cheque?
To explain, David Smith an Associate Professor of American Politics and Foreign Policy, at the United States Studies Centre at the University of Sydney spoke with ABC NewsRadio's Sarah Morice.
